title: King calls slave trade a 'shameful chapter' during Commonwealth address
description: King Charles has described the transatlantic slave trade as a "shameful chapter of history" that filled him with "profound sorrow" as he opened a summ
body: King Charles has described the transatlantic slave trade as a "shameful chapter of history" that filled him with "profound sorrow" as he opened a summit of Commonwealth leaders in the Caribbean.He said the trade in enslaved persons "still casts a shadow" over the association of nations.There have been calls from some for the UK to make a formal apology for its historic role in the slave trade ahead of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda, but there was not one in the King's address. Prime Minister Andy Burnham, also at the summit, has said that he is open to Britain issuing a formal apology but has ruled out financial reparations. While there was no direct apology, the King did offer some contrition - and there was also an acknowledgement that he had personally learnt more about the legacy of the slave trade.He said: "The transatlantic trade in enslaved persons still casts a shadow over these islands and other members of our Commonwealth. "As I have said before, that shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow."He told the summit: "The more I have furthered my own understanding of the issues, through listening, learning and looking, the more committed I have become to finding ways for us to work in modern partnership to address the wrongs of the past with action for the future."King Charles continued: "History is not ours to choose or to change. It is bequeathed to us in complex synthesis by forebears we can never know."Our inheritance includes both their achievements and their failures – the good they did as well as the wrongs."The King's address also referenced the "brutal conflicts" the world is facing, the "catastrophic reality" of climate and rapid technological development. The Chogm meeting gathers leaders from 56 states every two years in a different part of the Commonwealth, a voluntary grouping made up primarily of former territories of the British Empire. The biennial meeting's official theme this year is Accelerating Partnerships and Investment for a Prosperous Commonwealth.Speaking on Tuesday, Burnham said his government was bringing a new approach, aiming to "revitalise the Commonwealth", despite turning down demands for reparations."I've been very clear that we do not support reparations," he said. "But it's not the case that we don't support countries in the Commonwealth around development, and helping them with debt issues that they've got, green finance."That's what we've done under all governments and in my view we should continue to do as part of being a Commonwealth."The King and Queen are on a tour of the Caribbean which has reignited difficult debates over the UK's colonial legacy in the region.On his first stop in the Bahamas, the King delivered a speech in which he spoke of the "suffering of the past".In Guyana, he visited the site of a Slave Rebellion, where hundreds of enslaved people were killed.

schema.headline: King calls slave trade a 'shameful chapter' during Commonwealth address

title: Spanish transport minister resigns days after deadly train crash
description: Puente announced his decision at the end of a congressional session on Tuesday evening in which he had outlined new rail safety measures and been gril
body: Puente announced his decision at the end of a congressional session on Tuesday evening in which he had outlined new rail safety measures and been grilled by the opposition. He said he had taken the decision to resign immediately after the 28 October disaster, but had not made it public.Puente had been under mounting pressure in the wake of the disaster as opposition parties and some allies of the government called on him to step down.His resignation comes as a blow to the Socialist-led government ahead of a general election set for 29 November.During his lengthy hearing before lawmakers, Puente said: "I wish to inform you that I am not only stepping down from my position as minister of transport, but that I am also withdrawing my name from the lists for the early legislative elections."Leaked audio recordings published in Spanish media soon after the crash revealed conversations between train drivers and a control centre just minutes before the disaster. The three recordings of conversations between Madrid's control centre and two train drivers appear to show that one high-speed train was given clearance to move even though another train had stopped on the track, about 25km (15 miles) ahead.Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has said that authorities will "get to the bottom of every last detail of this tragedy".Last week's crash was one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013. The country observed three days of mourning after the tragedy.The moving train, run by state-owned operator Renfe, had 397 passengers on board. The stationary train was run by private operator Iryo, and carrying 147 passengers.A reported issue with the automatic signalling system - a computer failure - had forced all trains to halt on the affected stretch.But later the Renfe train was ordered to proceed in "error", according to Puente.The audio recordings were published by several Spanish news outlets including El Pais and RTVE.In one, a control centre operator is speaking to the driver of the Renfe train, which was having some technical difficulties. After some exchanges, the control operator tells the driver: "Continue your journey and then proceed under [Lateral Signalling Block], at normal speed with normal operation."The driver replies: "At normal speed?" To which the controller answers: "Yes."The Lateral Signalling Block is a back-up or alternative train system used when the automatic signalling or data transmission system fails.The driver of the stationary Iryo train says in another audio recording that communication with the train-control system has been lost, and it is not moving.The train "is stationary in front of the entry signal at Urda", the driver tells the control centre operator. After a series of exchanges, the driver is then told to "resume the journey" normally.The Iryo driver then contacts the control centre again, according to a later recording, saying they cannot start the train. "The train won't allow me to control the [security] system. That's why I am still stopped in front of the entry signal," they say.The latter recording suggests that the controller had been notified that the Iryo train remained stationary as the Renfe train approached.Iryo said its carriages were "struck from behind" by the other train.Puente said last week that the decision to instruct the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions, was "inexplicable".

schema.headline: Spanish transport minister resigns days after deadly train crash

title: UK also affected by cyber-attack which hit European fridges
description: Businesses in the UK's food supply chain have been impacted by the cyber-attack which hit supermarket fridges and freezers across Europe on Monday.The
body: Businesses in the UK's food supply chain have been impacted by the cyber-attack which hit supermarket fridges and freezers across Europe on Monday.The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says it is aware of "a couple of instances where vulnerable technology had been exploited in the UK."The NCSC's chief executive Dr Richard Horne told the Today programme, on BBC Radio Four, that it had "worked through the night" to alert potentially affected organisations in the UK.The British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers (AIMS) told the BBC some of its more than 300 members had unexpectedly become what it called "collateral" as part of the hacks.Two members saw their fridges begin to defrost, AIMS said, while another saw their cold units rise up to 100C (212F) in temperature.AIMS spokesman Tony Goodger said the affected devices were empty at the time so no produce was lost - but urged businesses to be vigilant.The incident "must act as a reminder to all in the food industry at whatever point in the supply chain they are that their businesses may be seen by some as targets," he said.On Monday, supermarkets in countries including Ireland, Sweden, Estonia, and Belgium reported fridges and freezers being hiked in temperature.The events followed attacks targeting supermarkets and food suppliers across France in early October.Hundreds of stores were targeted by the overnight hack, which spoiled fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.Those attacks exploited vulnerabilities in some systems used to remotely control and manage cold refrigeration units that had been surfaced by cyber-security researchers months prior.Horne told the BBC on Tuesday that it was still "too early to say" who was behind the hacks.But he said it pointed to an urgent need for organisations and businesses to ensure the technology underpinning a whole range of applications we use and need daily was secure and up-to-date."That technology base we rely on as a society has not been invested on to the extent it needs to be," Horne said, noting many firms had extended systems beyond their end of life, not upgraded them nor kept them in secure compartments  disconnected from the internet.Such actions can create vulnerabilities that many cyber-security experts say amounts to low-hanging fruit for hackers, and can be easily exploited. But the UK's cyber chief said that they could be found and exploited more quickly and easily via "AI in the hands of our adversaries"."We do need all organisations to look at what they rely on, to invest in renewal," he said."We intervene where we can. But, at the end of the day, it's your business. It's your charity. It's your life. You need to make the choice and choose wisely."Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected in Monday's cyber incident, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.Sabcobel, a Belgian company that manufactures some of the affected refrigerators, said the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode, causing them to warm up.The same method was thought to have been used in last month's incident that hit hundreds of French supermarkets.As with that incident, many of the retailers affected on Monday said they had no choice but to throw away spoiled food - some saying this amounted to hundreds of thousands of euro in lost produce.Mathieu Tilman, who runs a Delhaize supermarket in Belgium, told the BBC he found it "truly distressing"."There's so many people starving, people who don't have enough to eat. How can we end up throwing away so much food?""In moments like these, you just feel like quitting your job."So far, there have been little to no signs of any such impact in the UK.But the BBC has approached major UK supermarkets for comment and asked what action, if any, they are taking to safeguard against any similar hacks attempts."Retailers invest heavily in their cybersecurity and are currently working with the NCSC to ensure their fridges and freezers are secure as possible against potential attacks," said Graham Wynn, assistant director of regulatory affairs at the British Retail Consortium. Asda, Lidl, M&S, Sainsbury's and Tesco are among the retail trade association's members.Paul Chichester, director of operations at the NCSC, said at the launch of its annual report on Tuesday it was continuing to work with and monitor UK organisations affected."At the moment, the impact is minimal," he added. "We're working with organisations identifying existing vulnerabilities in the UK and trying to get those closed before somebody exploits them."

schema.headline: UK also affected by cyber-attack which hit European fridges

title: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor called to give evidence in fraud trial next month
description: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has been served with a summons compelling him to give evidence in a fraud trial in the High Court on or around 15 December,
body: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has been served with a summons compelling him to give evidence in a fraud trial in the High Court on or around 15 December, the BBC understandsThe witness summons will see him giving evidence and taking questions, in a case in which a wealthy woman alleges she was cheated by her former financial adviser.Mountbatten-Windsor is not accused of wrongdoing, but he could face difficult questions about his financial arrangements as it is said that he was in receipt of some of the disputed payments, including a transfer to him of £750,000.His court appearance will be the first public questioning Mountbatten-Windsor has faced since his BBC Newsnight interview in 2019.It is also believed that Mountbatten-Windsor is the first royal since the 19th Century to be sent such a witness summons.Such an unusual royal moment is likely to receive widespread media coverage - not least for the opportunity to hear the former Duke of York's first public comments since being stripped of his titles.Last month, a judge gave permission for Mountbatten-Windsor to be called as a witness.The summons was issued this week, with the case set to begin from mid-November and with Mountbatten-Windsor to appear as a witness around the 15 December, which is usually in person, but could be on video.There have been many questions in recent years about Mountbatten-Windsor's personal finances - and challenges about a lack of transparency - and this case promises to give a rare opportunity to hear his own explanations about his financial dealings.The case will hear allegations made by Nebahat Isbilen, an elderly Turkish woman, who says her former adviser Selman Turk misled her and used her wealth to his own advantage.Turk has strongly denied dishonesty.Mountbatten-Windsor will be asked to give evidence related to disputed questions about the handling of Isbilen's money.According to court documents, Isbilen claimed she was misled by Turk into paying £750,000 to Mountbatten-Windsor, believing it was for help with a passport.Turk has denied the allegation and says this payment was a gift made on Isbilen's own initiative to create goodwill with the then duke and had nothing to do with a passport.The case covers payments made at the very end of his time as a working royal.The transfer of money came the day after Mountbatten-Windsor recorded his BBC Newsnight interview, which was then broadcast the following night, and was soon followed by the then Duke of York stepping down from royal duties.In 2021, Isbilen's lawyers contacted the then Prince Andrew and the money had been paid back, but the forthcoming court case will consider claims about Turk's behaviour, with Mountbatten-Windsor set to be a significant witness.Court documents show there will be questions about another significant sum of money paid from Isbilen's account - around £768,000 in January 2020.Turk has claimed it was a loan to Mountbatten-Windsor for the purchase of a chalet in Switzerland - a suggestion which is contested by Isbilen and had been challenged in previous court hearings.Turk had met Mountbatten-Windsor in autumn 2019 through the Pitch@Palace project, a Dragon's Den-style pitching event run by the former duke. That had led to social gatherings, bringing together Turk and his family, Isbilen and the then Duke and Duchess of York.Justice Adam Johnson has said that, given the seriousness of the allegations, Turk should have access to "the evidence he considers relevant and material".That meant that Turk wanted to use Mountbatten-Windsor's evidence and has been successful in summonsing him for that purpose.Turk's representatives, Janes Solicitors, said he denies the claims of dishonesty and looks forward to being vindicated in court.Mountbatten-Windsor has been approached for a response.The trial at the High Court is expected to begin later this month.

schema.headline: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor called to give evidence in fraud trial next month

title: How 'mogging' went from toxic term to mainstream
description: "Mogging" has seen its usage soar over the past year, with the Gen Z slang term being named Collins English Dictionary's word of the year.Finding its
body: "Mogging" has seen its usage soar over the past year, with the Gen Z slang term being named Collins English Dictionary's word of the year.Finding its origins in the online language of the manosphere, an online community built around hyper-masculine and often misogynistic content, the term broke out into the mainstream this year, being used by celebrities and the media.The word is defined by Collins as being used playfully to mean "the act of outshining or outperforming someone or something" and is now widely employed in online discourse about celebrity culture, with signs it is making its way into everyday vocabulary."I heard someone the other day say they were 'walk-mogged' - basically just someone else in the street about their age walking faster than them," says Tony Thorne, a language consultant at King's College London.The term has grown in usage through its association with Clavicular, an influencer known for "looksmaxxing" content, who recently pleaded not guilty to charges including rape. He regularly posts clips of himself attempting to "mog" people in public spaces.The word reached a wider audience when posts describing the controversial streamer as having been "brutally frame mogged" went viral earlier this year.But "mogging" may be a lot older than its recent surge might suggest.Thorne explains that the term - often traced back to the acronym AMOG, or Alpha Male of the Group - was originally used in the 2010s on bodybuilding and incel (involuntary celibate) message boards, before being co-opted by a younger, broader audience."They started to diffuse it," he says."It was a toxic term about extreme competitiveness, the urge to dominate. People then started to use it ironically and teasingly."In a nod to its origins, Hollywood royalty and seven-time Mr Olympia, Arnold Schwarzenegger, posted footage of himself in his bodybuilding heyday earlier this year, along with the ironic caption "someone just tried to explain this new trend 'frame mogging' to me...", external.Slang terms breaking out of the community that coins them isn't unprecedented."It's becoming more like the drag queen slang that was also used until recently - 'it was lit', 'she slays', 'he's a king', 'she's a queen'. It's become part of that more sort of silly, kind celebrity-type banter," says Thorne.He believes that the term has now "largely been detoxified" as it mostly "retains that tinge of mockery or irony"."I can't speak for all the instances when it's used, but for young people I know who are using it today, there is not anything unhealthy about it anymore."Reflecting this softer and more mainstream meaning, British Vogue captioned their photo of Heated Rivalry actor Hudson Williams arriving at the 2026 Golden Globes as him "mogging at the Golden Globes". And in an interview earlier this year, figure skater Alysa Liu said her "main goal for this competition was to mog". At its heart, there still remains a competitive element to how the word is used to frame a situation."The language still retains this element of hyper-individual, competitive performance culture. It's still got that element," says Thorne. A recent online debate was sparked between fans comparing People magazine's choice for 2026's sexiest man alive, The Pitt actor Noah Wyle, with the 2025 winner, Wicked star Jonathan Bailey. Last year, fans of Zara Larsson and Tate McRae pitched the two singers against each other after the Swedish popstar opened for McRae on the North American leg of latter's Miss Possessive tour. Some fans viewed Larsson's performance as having "mogged" McRae, despite being a support act.Larsson later pushed back on the comparison, speaking about her respect for McRae during an interview on the Call Her Daddy podcast. Another famous face that has been brought into the mogging debate is Cillian Murphy, with the Irish actor being compared favourably to his co-stars by some.

schema.headline: How 'mogging' went from toxic term to mainstream

title: Alex Mitchell: England scrum-half ruled out of Nations Championship
description: Tommy Freeman, Mitchell's team-mate for club and country, said it was "gutting" news for his colleague but backed him to come back stronger."It will d
body: Tommy Freeman, Mitchell's team-mate for club and country, said it was "gutting" news for his colleague but backed him to come back stronger."It will definitely give him time to go after his rehab and get to the bottom of what is going on, find new solutions and ways to maximise his recovery," Saints wing Freeman said."You don't want to see your mate and a player who is a massive part of this group out. He is going to be missed with his humour off the field and playing ability on it."Freeman said Smith is "pretty optimistic" about playing against the Wallabies and despite a reduced role in training is making up for it in other areas."He's joining in with meetings and giving good points so he's very much involved and that shows the character he is," he added.Bath's Ben Spencer and Bristol Bears' Harry Randall were called in as scrum-half options on Monday, with Leicester's Jack van Poortvliet - who started all three of England's summer Tests - the likely first-choice nine.Northampton scrum-half Archie McParland, 21, was named in the initial training squad but has withdrawn with a calf injury.Hooker Luke Cowan-Dickie and flanker Tom Curry both took part in modified training on Tuesday at England's Bagshot base, but are expected to be fit for selection.England boss Steve Borthwick will name his side to face Australia on Friday.

title: Death toll rises in Ukraine after Russia attacks aid centre, hospice and hospital
description: Russian strikes on Ukraine – including on an aid centre, a hospice and a hospital – have killed at least 38 civilians and injured scores of others ove
body: Russian strikes on Ukraine – including on an aid centre, a hospice and a hospital – have killed at least 38 civilians and injured scores of others over the last 24 hours.At least 33 people are known to have died in a glide bomb attack in the southern Zaporizhzhia region on Monday night, and President Volodymyr Zelensky said the number of victims was set to rise as more than 50 people could be trapped under the rubble.He called the strike in Komyshuvakha village "one of the largest mass killings committed by Russia during this war".Ukraine had proposed to extend and expand last week's ceasefire in the Kherson region which allowed people from the frontline Russian-occupied town of Oleshky to evacuate, Zelensky added.The attack on a school building being used as an aid distribution centre in Komyshuvakha was Moscow's response, he said.Elsewhere, a hospice was attacked in the central city of Dnipro and a hospital was hit in the north-eastern city of Kharkiv, where Zelensky said 73 people were wounded, most of them elderly patients.Nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit Komyshuvakha as residents were gathering to receive humanitarian aid at a distribution centre, authorities said. Local media reported that when the attack began, people took refuge underground but the roof  collapsed, trapping many underneath. "The scale of the tragedy is difficult to comprehend," regional head Mykhailo Semikin said.Russia's defense ministry said the attack had targeted Ukrainian military units and killed 25 servicemen. However, there was no credible evidence that the site was being used by the Ukrainian military and there were no major military or industrial facilities in the settlement of Komyshuvakha, reports BBC News Russian defence correspondent Ilya Abishev.The village is to the south-east of the city of Zaporizhzhia, which has come under constant Russian bombardment. According to Abishev, Komyshuvakha is of high military importance as part of Ukraine's defensive and transport network on the approaches to the regional capital. But the UN's human rights monitoring mission said the distribution of humanitarian aid at the local school had been highly publicised and the attack "seems to have violated the most fundamental principles of international humanitarian law", external."I realise that I am violating ethics," wrote Filatov. "I want as many people as possible to see these photos. Especially politicians and diplomats. Especially abroad."These are elderly, terminally ill people. This is a Russian missile."Elsewhere in Dnipro, a separate strike killed two people and left 18 others wounded. Another five people were killed in aerial bomb and drone strikes on Ukraine's eastern Donetsk region.Russia has also struck energy infrastructure in nine regions, affecting water and heating. The water supply in Kyiv was entirely cut off "due to enemy attacks and damage to the capital's energy infrastructure", the main water supplier Kyivvodokanal said. The entire metro network was suspended on Tuesday and Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the situation surrounding the city's power supply was becoming "very difficult".As Ukraine was counting its dead, the Kremlin announced it would take part in three-way peace talks with Ukraine brokered by the US in Abu Dhabi on 10-11 November.It will be the first trilateral meeting since February. Since then, Russia and the US have begun engaging more directly, with US President Donald Trump announcing a deal to import Russian diesel.Speaking to reporters in Berlin on Tuesday, Zelensky said that it was important for Russia to engage seriously in negotiations on a ceasefire and a peaceful settlement, but that he had so far had not seen "any indication" of that being the case.Several rounds of ceasefire talks late last year yielded no results, and in public declarations Russian officials have generally refused to budge from Moscow's maximalist demand of effective Ukrainian surrender.US First Lady Melania Trump Melania Trump, who was credited with brokering a truce last week in the besieged town of Oleshky, is set to host representatives of Russia and Ukraine at the White House on Thursday. However, no details were given in the White House statement of who was due to attend the meeting., externalThe UN said last month that civilian casualties in Ukraine had reached a "record level", as Russian armed forces resumed systematic attacks on energy infrastructure.Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Its advances on the front line have since stalled, and attacks on Ukraine have intensified, with Moscow employing large numbers of missiles and drones to strike Ukrainian cities. At the same time, Ukraine is faces a critical air defense shortage due to stalled Western deliveries of weapons and a lack of American Patriot interceptor missiles.In Berlin, Zelensky acknowledged that although the front line was stable "the situation in the air was not as positive, particularly when it comes to our air defence capabilities and the protection of our civilian population".

schema.headline: Death toll rises in Ukraine after Russia attacks aid centre, hospice and hospital

title: William Saliba's return gives Mikel Arteta selection headache at Arsenal
description: Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta will soon have a big defensive dilemma.But it is one that will be both welcome to the Arsenal boss and the envy of other top
body: Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta will soon have a big defensive dilemma.But it is one that will be both welcome to the Arsenal boss and the envy of other top teams across the continent.That's because William Saliba - a key figure in the Gunners' title win last season - is back in training, having missed the entire campaign so far because of a back injury following his early withdrawal in France's World Cup semi-final loss to Spain.The 25-year-old has been one of the Premier League's top defenders in recent seasons but - in his absence - summer signing Ezri Konsa has stepped in seamlessly to help Arsenal back to the top of the table.Indeed, since Konsa's arrival from Aston Villa for £55m, he and Gabriel Magalhaes  have struck up a formidable partnership, with Arsenal again boasting the league's tightest defence, conceding just five goals in nine games.Saliba had been managing his back issue throughout last season but was sent to see a specialist after the World Cup. It was decided he did not need to undergo surgery but would require a lengthy rehabilitation. No timescale on his return was set. The France international had been doing individual training at Arsenal's base but has now returned to full training before their Champions League meeting with Slavia Prague and then, a busy festive schedule looming. Saliba and regular partner Gabriel were a huge reason why the Gunners won the Premier League title for the first time in 22 years last season.Their partnership was the bedrock of Arteta's team, which conceded only 27 league goals. Saliba was then named in the PFA team of the year for the fourth consecutive time. Arsenal have always said that they will be cautious with Saliba's return but his return to fitness will leave Arteta with some tough choices to make in his backline. Such was Arsenal's strength in defence, there were questions about whether they needed to sign Konsa when the Gunners decided to spend £55m on the England international.But the centre-back has been one of the club's best players this season as they sit top of the Premier League. Some have even suggested Konsa and Gabriel have become the best partnership in world football, external.Arsenal already had seven senior defenders when they signed Konsa including one of the most solid and well-established partnerships in world football in Saliba and Gabriel.But in Saliba's absence, Konsa has started seven of Arsenal's nine Premier League matches, having joined just hours before their opening match against Coventry before coming on against former club Aston Villa for his debut. And Arteta has said the way that Konsa has settled for the Gunners has been "unbelievable". The defender made 286 appearances for Villa after joining in July 2019 from Brentford and helped them win the Europa League in May, the club's first European trophy since 1982.He has established himself as a first-choice starter for England and started seven of the eight games the Three Lions played at the World Cup. And what could now prove a big clue to his Arsenal future - he started the quarter-final against Norway at right back. Konsa is an imposing figure, quick across the ground, and his aggression in challenges has impressed supporters.The 29-year-old scored the opener against Everton in Arsenal's 2-0 win and put in another commanding performance as the Gunners beat Liverpool at Anfield for the first time in 14 years on Sunday.Arsenal host Hull on Saturday before the next international break starts this month. That time will allow Saliba to further build up his fitness before he will become a regular option again for Arteta. However, when Saliba does return, Arteta is going to have to disappoint someone.Ben White and Jurrien Timber have been Arsenal's first choice right-backs this season and are dependable top-level options. Both have previously had fitness issues but White has been available for all but one of Arsenal's games this campaign.Konsa could move to right-back, a position he also made his England debut in, which would allow Saliba to slot in next to Gabriel in his regular spot. Arteta values physicality in his Arsenal side and moving Konsa, who is physically imposing, to right-back would give opposition attackers a formidable challenge. Saliba's return also lowers the chance of game time for young centre-back Cristhian Mosquera and his low number of minutes so far this season will raise questions about his future, even though he has recovered from a hamstring injury. The Gunners played 63 games in all competitions last season as they won the league and reached the Champions League final. And, with Arteta aiming to defend the title and have European success this time out, there will be a lot of games for him to rotate his many options.

schema.headline: William Saliba's return gives Mikel Arteta selection headache at Arsenal

title: Americans vote in midterms that could define Trump's closing chapter
description: Americans head to the polls for elections that could define Trump's closing chapterImage source, Getty ImagesByNorth America editorUpdated 09:29 GMTWi
body: Americans head to the polls for elections that could define Trump's closing chapterImage source, Getty ImagesByNorth America editorUpdated 09:29 GMTWith two years of his presidency remaining, Donald Trump, who has dominated American politics over the past decade and transformed it in remarkable ways, is facing potentially pivotal elections.And the midterm elections on Tuesday that will decide control of Congress come at a difficult moment for his Republican Party. Voters overwhelmingly say they are most concerned about the cost of living. Food and fuel prices have soared in part due to the president's aggressive tariffs and unpopular war with Iran, so it will be top of mind as many head to the polls.Trump, who has faced record low approval ratings in recent months, has been campaigning hard, headlining dozens of rallies across the country.He made his closing pitch on Monday in front of the Reflecting Pool in Washington DC, which has been the subject of a controversial renovation. Looking back at the midterms campaign, he said Republicans "gave this a very strong shot".But ahead of the vote, high prices are a concern for voters on all sides - which helps explain why he has been campaigning in previously safe Republican territory, appearing in Iowa and Kansas during a final weekend blitz.His party has also poured hundreds of millions of dollars of campaign advertising into these traditionally safe contests, such as the Senate race in Kansas."When they start spending hard American dollars on political advertising in a state that they should be winning, that's how you know that they think they're in trouble," Carrie Dann, the managing editor of the Cook Political Report, which analyses campaigns and elections, told the BBC."The spending [in Kansas] is going to be far more than Republicans ever anticipated," she added. That points to a party that is approaching these elections on the defensive.Figure caption, Trump targets midterm voters with final campaign speech at Reflecting PoolAt many of his rallies, Trump has also made a plea to voters. "In this election, I'm asking you to pretend, please, that I'm on the ballot," he said last month. "Just pretend."Of course, he is not on the ballot. But this plea - which he made again in Iowa on Sunday - gets to the heart of a critical question: Is he still an electoral asset for his Republican Party?The answer to that is not as simple as it once was.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Trump held a rally in Kansas, a traditionally safe Republican state, on Sunday as polls suggest the Senate race may be in play for DemocratsTrump returned to the White House as a formidable force following his crushing 2024 election win - and had the healthy approval ratings to match. Before that, during the previous midterm elections in 2022, his endorsement was courted by Republicans who saw it as vital to success.Now, with the war with Iran dragging on and hitting many Americans in the pocket, his approval ratings have sunk. The price of a gallon of diesel - which was $3.75 before the war started in February - hit a record high of $6.52 in September."I literally just had my son drive across the country, and he called me in every state and told me the price of gas," one voter in Iowa told me. "And I was like - 'oh my gosh, this is horrible'."Inflation has also ticked up from 3% when Trump took office to 3.7% today, and economists estimate it would have been lower without his sweeping regime of global tariffs.There is concern among Republicans that this economic picture has left them vulnerable in typically safe races, in states such as Texas, Ohio and Kansas."The southern states, the midwestern states, the American heartland - that is where Republicans tend to thrive," said Stephen Hawkins, the global director of research at the pollster More in Common. "But that is where the Senate races that are so interesting are playing out right now.""Places where President Trump won by 10, 12, 15 points just two years ago in the presidential race are now states where Democrats have a very viable chance of taking a Senate seat," he said.Figure caption, Voter voices: Which issues matter most to Americans?When I asked voters in Iowa, a state Trump won in 2024 that has been hit by soaring fuel and fertiliser costs, whether the president would make people more or less likely to back Republicans - the answer was revealing."With the current climate, I would think possibly less, believe it or not," Paul Ross told me outside a busy college football game. "As a Republican myself, I would think it might be detrimental.""I think it definitely puts voters off, there's no doubt about that, and I do think it probably raises the Democratic side to a level that isn't always there, just because it's Donald Trump," added Zach Shimp."He's got us in the war," another voter, Rose Heming, said. "Prices and groceries [are] high - sky high - gas is sky high."That is the story of this election. Many voters, including in solidly Republican states, are hurting financially and polls suggest they may want to make this known at the ballot box on Tuesday.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Millions of Americans voted early - and millions more will head to the polls throughout TuesdayBut it is too simplistic to think this backdrop of war, tariffs and soaring prices will usher in a thumping Democratic victory in the House, Senate and governors' races.Many Republican voters are angry with the president, but not so angry that they would vote for a Democrat. It is a mistake to assume that Trump's weak approval ratings translate to increasing popularity for the other side.In fact, final polls taken before the elections suggest Trump's approval rating is around 38%. That is low - but the same polls, including a national NBC poll released on Sunday, external, indicate that only 29% of voters view the Democratic Party positively. Voter frustration is no guarantee of a willingness to switch sides on Tuesday."We like to stay out of people's business," Tim McKinnon, a Republican in Iowa who voted for Trump in 2024 told me last month. "And so [Trump's] world stage interventions time after time after time - we don't love it."We didn't expect him to necessarily be a perfect choir boy obviously," his wife, Michelle, added. "We voted for the underbelly of what he was standing for."The Democratic Party cannot rely on voters like the McKinnons, who are frustrated with elements of Trump's recent agenda, to back them. They do not think Democrats will ever reflect their Christian, conservative values."One dollar more on gas is not going to change what we believe in," Tim McKinnon told me.Figure caption, 'My vote still matters' - Americans weigh in on the power of their ballotIf Democrats do win a large swathe of seats on Tuesday night, it won't necessarily be because voters love them – they just hate them a little less.The party, however, is already looking ahead to a 2028 presidential election in which they will have to unite behind a single candidate. That is easier said than done given their clear fractures - some of which spilled out publicly during this election cycle, including in Michigan over the weekend.Democrats will be closely watching these results for lessons ahead of 2028. Can they really win in Texas? Can they tempt rural voters in deep Republican strongholds? And will some of their rising stars, such as Jon Ossoff in Georgia and James Talarico in Texas, live up to the hype?If the answer to some of these questions is no, there will be much to ponder for the party over the next year. And the post-mortem may not be pretty."This represents an opportunity, really, for Democrats to expand a lot of their influence, not just in terms of numbers, but in terms of perception of where they can compete," Hawkins, from the pollster More in Common, said.GUIDE: What are the US midterms?IN DEPTH: The real reasons there are so few young US politicians EXPLORE: Where the US midterms will be won and lostVERIFY: How the US economy is really doing under TrumpNEWSLETTER: Sign up for Anthony Zurcher's analysis in your inboxRepublican attempts, including from Trump himself, to paint the Democrats as dangerous communists have not landed with all voters.In Detroit, Michigan, Nicole Williams - who owns her own hairdressing salon - summed up the view of many people I spoke to. "Anything is better than what we have now," she said. "Socialist? Socialised? It don't matter to me. Lower my cost of living.""People are just tired of the disrespect to Americans, because he is an American," Gwen Jackson, another Michigan voter, said, referring to the state's left-wing Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed who Trump has repeatedly attacked."People are just tired," she said. "They're ready to see a change."Even when a sitting president is more popular than Trump, their party usually loses seats in the midterms. This, combined with the latest polling, means there is confidence among Democrats that they will at least win the House of Representatives."It's the cost of living, it's the undeclared war," Democratic strategist Mary Anne Marsh said of the key issues. "Every Republican who did not stand up to Donald Trump is about to realise the consequences of believing he was invincible."If the Democrats do win the House, the party could try to block any legislation Trump wants to pass. That is unlikely to worry him, given he has already tried to bypass Congress as much as possible and rule by signing executive orders from the Oval Office instead.Trump will be more concerned about the investigations Democrats will be able to launch if they take control of the House. They may also try to impeach some of his cabinet members, with Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth seen as a likely candidate due to the war in Iran.Figure caption, Watch: What's at stake for President Trump in the US midterms?Winning the Senate on Tuesday is likely to be a much harder task for Democrats.Thirty-five seats are up for election, and they will need a net gain of four to win control. If they lose in Michigan - a battleground seat they already hold - they will need a net gain of five seats to win it.Most of the battleground races are close and several sit within the margin of error for pollsters. The crucial Senate races to watch are in Michigan, Texas, Ohio, Iowa, Maine, Alaska and North Carolina. This is, in reality, where these midterm elections will be won and lost.There is, as always with American elections, an important caveat around the polls. They have historically overestimated the Democratic Party and underestimated President Trump, who appears convinced that he can once again defy them.But if the polls are close to correct about the suggested surge of support for Democrats, then he could be looking at painful defeats in states that have been reliable Republican strongholds for decades.How Trump may respond to any stinging losses is an open question. He has repeatedly questioned the integrity and security of these elections, and the possibility that he does so again as votes are still being counted or when results are declared is a very real one.These elections, however, represent a hugely significant moment for Americans, many of whom want to see real change over the next two years.For both parties, they will serve as the final electoral test before a 2028 presidential election that will determine what a post-Trump politics looks and feels like. And for the president himself, they are an opportunity for voters to cast judgement on how he and his party are performing.As Trump looks to shape his legacy in the next two years, the question is whether a change in control of Congress, which he has largely bypassed, would really curb his presidency at all.Get in touchWhat are your questions about the midterms? Get in touch.

schema.headline: Americans vote in midterms that could define Trump's closing chapter

title: West Ham approach Scott Parker after sacking Nuno Espirito Santo
description: Image source, ShutterstockImage caption, Scott Parker (right) would be West Ham's fourth permanent manager since May 2024 if he succeeds Nuno Espirito
body: Image source, ShutterstockImage caption, Scott Parker (right) would be West Ham's fourth permanent manager since May 2024 if he succeeds Nuno Espirito Santo (left)ByBrent PilnickBBC Sport England and Sami MokbelSenior football correspondentUpdated 8 hours agoWest Ham United are expected to appoint Scott Parker as head coach after sacking Nuno Espirito Santo.The 52-year-old Portuguese has paid the price for West Ham's disappointing start to the Championship season, having overseen their relegation from the Premier League last season.BBC Sport understands that the club are in advanced talks with former Burnley, Bournemouth and Fulham boss Parker and he could be confirmed before Wednesday's Championship trip to Cardiff City.The former England midfielder had four seasons as a player with the Hammers and led Bournemouth and Burnley to promotion from the Championship as a manager.Widely seen as favourites for automatic promotion, the London side are currently eighth in the table, six points behind leaders Middlesbrough.They have won two of their past six games and have lost back-to-back home matches - going down 3-2 to Southampton and then 3-1 to West Bromwich Albion on Saturday - losses that have seen them drop down from second place.Assistant head coach Rui Pedro Silva and goalkeeper coach Rui Barbosa have also left the club.Mark Noble, Steve Potts and Gerard Prenderville will take temporary charge of the side for their Championship trip to Cardiff City on Wednesday night. "Following a thorough review of the start to the EFL Championship season, the board of directors believe that a change is necessary at this time in order to ensure that the club's objectives and expectations remain on track," a West Ham United statement read. "West Ham United would like to thank Nuno, Rui and Rui for their hard work and commitment during their time at the club, and wish them all the very best for the future."The process of recruiting a new head coach is already under way."Image source, ShutterstockImage caption, Nuno Espirito Santo's last win as West Ham boss came at Swansea CityThe decision means West Ham are looking for their fourth permanent manager since David Moyes left London Stadium in May 2024.His successor Julen Lopetegui was sacked after just six months in charge with the Hammers mid-table having won six of their 20 Premier League matches.He was replaced by former Chelsea and Brighton boss Graham Potter, who oversaw a 14th-placed finish, but was sacked after only eight months in charge with the club 19th in the table.The club opted to stick with former Wolves and Tottenham Hotspur boss Nuno despite him being unable to turn around the club's fortunes. They were relegated at the end of last season after finishing two points behind Spurs. Despite that, this season had a troubled start for the Hammers - they failed to win any of their first three league matches and were 19th in the table.A run of four successive wins in the first half of September, where they scored 16 goals and went top of the table, appeared to show they had adapted to the second tier, with a 6-0 win over Wrexham the highlight of the run.Just two league victories have come since - a 6-0 win at nine-man Lincoln City and a 1-0 victory at Swansea City followed draws with London rivals Millwall and QPR. A squad that Parker can work with?Image source, ShutterstockImage caption, Scott Parker has been out of work since losing his job after Burnley were relegated from the Premier League in MayHaving posted losses of more than £104m, relegation meant West Ham had to sell players over the summer.The departures of the likes of Mateus Fernandes, Crysencio Summerville, El Hadji Malick Diouf, James Ward-Prowse and Freddie Potts secured the club about £150m in transfer revenue.They used some of that cash to pay Celtic a Championship record £22m for midfielder Arne Engels and spent a reported £12m on Norwegian winger Edvin Austbo. Experienced campaigners Joel Veltman and Manor Solomon also joined on free transfers from Brighton and Tottenham respectively while they kept key players such as England winger Jarrod Bowen, Czech midfielder Tomas Soucek and Greek defender Konstantinos Mavropanos.Soucek missed the first two months of the season with an ankle injury while some of their other signings have yet to deliver. Engels has three assists and no goals in 12 games while Austbo has scored twice and had two assists having started just two league matches.It is a squad that is capable of turning things around, especially under a manager with Championship promotion experience such as Parker. Figure caption, West Ham fan excited by expected arrival of Scott Parker'West Ham's hierarchy feel Parker understands the club'Image source, ShutterstockImage caption, Scott Parker guided Burnley to promotion from the Championship in April 2024Analysis - Simon Stone, BBC Sport chief football news reporterGiven the estimated £200m loss in revenue it is imperative the club goes straight back up to the Premier League.Two wins in six, a run which has dropped West Ham to eighth in the table, four points off second-placed Swansea in the final automatic promotion place, is not good enough.Scott Parker is the obvious choice as replacement and West Ham are wasting no time in getting the deal done.Parker made 129 appearances in a four-year stint with the Hammers. He won the club's player of the year award three times and was at West Ham when he was named Football Writers' Association player of the year in 2011.West Ham's hierarchy feel Parker understands the club and the culture and is someone the fans can get behind.Equally as important, he has already been promoted from the Championship three times, at Fulham, Bournemouth and Burnley.West Ham will hope he makes it number four next May.Image source, ShutterstockImage caption, West Ham have lost their past two games at homeAnalysis - Phil Parry, BBC Radio London sport editorThere were some who thought that Nuno would leave the club in the summer after they failed to survive their relegation battle, but the stability that he offered and his experience of guiding Wolves out of the Championship were seen as positive reasons to welcome his continuation at the helm.The 6-0 thumpings handed out to Wrexham and Lincoln are contrasted with some disappointing home defeats, including the past two outings at London Stadium.One of the major concerns has been the slow starts to games. They have conceded the opening goal in four of their past six in the Championship and have picked up just two points from those matches. It has been suggested that the team just don't appear to appreciate the intensity and urgency of games at this level and are still a little too ponderous in the first half.The Hammers have just been through a run of matches against teams who are in good form and are sitting high in the table, but losses in two of those games, both at home, have proven costly for Nuno.With the squad at their disposal and the fanbase that backs them, it will be an attractive job for the next head coach, but whoever it is will be aware that the expectation at London Stadium is for an immediate return to the Premier League and falling short of that objective is risky for long-term prospects.

schema.headline: West Ham approach Scott Parker after sacking Nuno Espirito Santo

title: Binance says fake job interviews used as part of $6.3bn crypto hack
description: Hackers who stole a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from Binance used fake job interviews and a compromised internal AI tool, the firm has revealed.Initial fin
body: Hackers who stole a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from Binance used fake job interviews and a compromised internal AI tool, the firm has revealed.Initial findings published by the company, which operates the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said hackers gained access to its systems through "sophisticated, multi-stage campaign".It said they used a range of techniques such as malicious software downloads to compromise the computers of Binance engineers and gain control over tools to drain its wallet of billions of dollars worth of crypto.Binance called it a "serious and highly sophisticated security incident" and apologised, saying "this should not have happened".In a post on X, external, Binance said hackers targeted its engineers using social engineering techniques.These see hackers use approaches such as phishing to trick people into parting with sensitive or personal details, that can then be used to try and access their accounts.Binance said as part of the hack, one of its engineers was contacted through a legitimate job-hunting platform and invited to bogus job interviews with fake company representatives.It said the perpetrators used "more advanced and deceptive" methods to build trust with him, such as sharing social media accounts that contained personal images.The engineer in question was instructed to download malware masquerading as an "assignment" during a second interview, that deployed malicious code with "obfuscation techniques" evading detection. Binance said hackers then leveraged the engineer's compromised computer and a compromised internal AI tool in October to gain control over two other engineers' laptops, and execute the next steps of the attack.The incident led Binance to suspend withdrawals for customers globally, meaning users could not get their cryptocurrency out of the platform until the service was restored on Sunday.Customers withdrew billions of dollars worth of assets after it reopened."We apologise for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry," it said.The company added it had taken a range of steps following the incident, including working with law enforcement to trace and freeze affected assets.It said it had also set aside more than 100% of the funds needed to cover the loss, noting 98% of the token assets impacted had been "replenished" as of Saturday.The record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) attack is thought to be the largest crypto hack to date.US crime agencies, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and Secret Service, have been assisting Binance in tracing the crypto taken from the platform's own wallets.The agencies, along with a range of cyber analysts, said that the hack - like similar breaches before it - bore the signs of having been orchestrated by North Korea.Pyongyang hit back at the claims on Tuesday, denying it was behind the hack.Kim Yo Jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said on the accusations were another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage North Korea's public image.The country has consistently denied being behind a number of major cyber attacks it has been blamed for in recent years.The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.Binance had previously not responded to the BBC's queries about North Korea's alleged involvement in the hack. But on Tuesday, the company wrote in its post on X, external: "The latest information released by the Federal Bureau of Investigation indicates that the Democratic People's Republic of Korea is responsible for this incident."As part of its security efforts following the attack, Binance said it would also  increase investment in AI tools that can detect security threats, as well as engage third-party cyber experts to carry out a full-scale review of the incident.It also said that it would seek to stablish a security research fund and work with leading AI and security firms on targeted initiatives.

schema.headline: Binance says fake job interviews used as part of $6.3bn crypto hack

title: Celebrity loses injunction bid but will stay anonymous pending appeal
description: A celebrity who asked the High Court to permanently prevent two news organisations from publishing his identity and allegations of sexual misconduct h
body: A celebrity who asked the High Court to permanently prevent two news organisations from publishing his identity and allegations of sexual misconduct has lost his case, with the court saying the man's claim for an injunction was denied.But the judge said a temporary injunction preventing the man from being named and the allegations published should remain in place, in order to allow the celebrity to appeal against the judgment, with anonymity and reporting restrictions remaining in force during the period allowed for any appeal.ITN and the Guardian have said they believe it is in the public interest to publish allegations that the man abused his status to engage, or attempt to engage, in "inappropriate sexual activities with a large number of girls and young women".The man, who denies the allegations, said any publication would be "highly likely" to lead him to kill himself, and that the court should prevent any publication or broadcast.In his judgment on Tuesday, Mr Justice Nicklin rejected the injunction request.He said: "The court did not determine whether the allegations, or any of them, were true, and the dismissal of the claim does not amount to approval of any publication the defendants may decide to make."Nicklin noted that the man has repeatedly said he intends to take his own life if the allegations are published, and that this must be taken seriously.He added these statements do not "establish that suicide is inevitable or that treatment cannot reduce the risk".With a strict anonymity order remaining in place, it would be against the law to identify the man or publish details that might do so.The man can now take his case to the Court of Appeal. Sara Mansoori KC, representing the celebrity, asked the court for time to decide whether he wanted to challenge the ruling.She said that her client is "in a highly vulnerable position" and has "not been in a position to give us instructions on any appeal".The claimant must lodge reasons to appeal by 16:30 GMT on 9 November.The case raises highly unusual legal issues concerning whether a court should stop publication when an individual claims that a media investigation would lead to them inflicting harm on themselves.The celebrity first asked the court in the summer to stop the publication of the investigation after journalists contacted him with allegations about this sexual activities with a large number of young women.ITN and the Guardian said their investigation had uncovered how the celebrity had allegedly abused his "power and status".During last week's application for a permanent injunction, Mansoori said making the allegations public would have a "potentially fatal impact".The barrister told the court that the man had tried to kill himself after he had been contacted by the media organisations and was later detained in hospital for his own protection - but later absconded and tried a second time to end his life.Those incidents of self-harm had not been because of the allegations themselves but the result of "long-term trauma and the fear of trial by media", she argued."The only reason [suicide attempts] would not be fatal is because the claimant would be locked up and prevented from his desire to end his life," she said.Lawyers for the media groups argued that there was a strong public interest in allowing their investigation to be publicised because of the serious nature of the allegations.In his judgment, Nicklin wrote: "The proposed publications concern serious allegations about the conduct of a prominent person and the alleged  use of status, influence and access in dealings with women and girls."The subject matter includes alleged abuse of power, sexual misconduct and inappropriate conduct towards younger or vulnerable persons."Those are matters capable of making a significant contribution to public debate."The celebrity argued that publishing the allegations would breach his protections under the European Convention on Human Rights, including articles that guarantee the right to life and protection from inhuman or degrading treatment.However, the judge rejected the claim that publication would violate the man's right to life, writing: "No prior case establishes that the Court's knowledge of a suicide risk, together with its power to prohibit the event expected to increase that risk, is by itself enough to require the Court to act."The judge accepted that publishing would cause the man "acute and potentially prolonged mental suffering" – but said "established law did not impose a positive obligation upon the Court to prevent that suffering by restraining publication".The man also cited the right to private and family life.While the judge acknowledged that publication "would interfere exceptionally seriously with the Claimant's private and family life", he also rejected that claim, saying a permanent injunction "would have been an exceptionally serious restriction upon freedom of expression".The BBC Action Line website has information about organisations that can offer support for the issues raised in this story.

schema.headline: Celebrity loses injunction bid but will stay anonymous pending appeal

title: Halloween: Bonfire attack victim has 'serious burns'
description: Independent councillor Paul Gallagher has spoken to the boy's mother and said she is "distraught". "Young people have gone to the bonfire and in the c
body: Independent councillor Paul Gallagher has spoken to the boy's mother and said she is "distraught". "Young people have gone to the bonfire and in the chaos of it, a young 17-year-old got knocked unconscious, fell onto a fire which at best can be described as white hot," Gallagher told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme. "I've spoken to his mother who was very distraught, to say the least."Gallagher said the boy will now require extensive medical care and it will take a long time for him to recover."The chaos around a bonfire is madness and it should never have happened that a young boy gets knocked out and put on a fire."Bonfires bring very little benefit, they are destructive, they are a serious danger to young people."The police are stepping up their hunt for the boy's attacker but no arrests have been made.They have appealed for witnesses to come forward, including anyone who may have captured the attack on their mobile phones.

schema.headline: Halloween: Bonfire attack victim has 'serious burns'

title: Florida plane crash investigators say jet may have broken apart before impact as family named
description: Investigators believe parts of a private jet that crashed in Florida and killed all nine onboard may have broken off while it was in the air.The Learj
body: Investigators believe parts of a private jet that crashed in Florida and killed all nine onboard may have broken off while it was in the air.The Learjet 60 had been bound for the Bahamas from Austin, Texas when it nosedived into a multi-lane highway and exploded on impact.A tech entrepreneur and his young family, as well as the 20-year-old co-pilot, were among those who died on Sunday.The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said weather conditions would be a major focus of the investigation but that it was struggling to access the wreckage due to the huge crater created by the jet on the road in Palm Beach.The plane crashed on Military Trail, a six-lane road that features businesses and restaurants, at around 12:50 local time (17:50 GMT)."The biggest obstacle that we're going to have is recovering the major wreckage from the impacted crater on the roadway," lead investigator Tim Monville said at a news conference on Monday.The NTSB said the crater, near the entrance to a mobile home park, had become partially filled with water because of severe storms. Heavy rainfall and thunderstorms had been reported in the area at the time of the crash.Debris was scattered across sports fields, businesses and homes in the area."We do have some evidence that there was some breakup of the aircraft before impact," the NTSB's Tom Chapman said. "We may find parts of the aircraft some distance away from the actual impact site."Officials are also trying to find out whether a cockpit voice recorder was onboard at the time of the crash and whether it can be recovered.Flight analysis indicates that the jet was plummeting hundreds of feet per second before it crashed.In air traffic control audio recordings, someone in the cockpit can be heard reporting "moderate turbulence" and that the crew was "managing the ice".They can then be heard saying the plane was "picking up precipitation" and "we need to climb". Moments later, the same voice said the plane was descending at a rate of 10,000ft (3,048m) per minute.An emergency was declared and they can be heard yelling "we are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000ft per minute", before saying, "we are going to crash into the ground".Seven passengers died on board, named in a joint statement as tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife Helen Sharp, and their two children - Emma, four, and Charlie, two - as well as friends of the family Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, and nanny Anita Maria Cetina. The pilot was named in media reports as 55-year-old Jeffrey Gregory, while Nathalia Filgueiras, 20, who earned her pilot's licence when she was 17, was reported to be the co-pilot.One man in a car on the ground sustained a leg injury.Nathalia Filgueiras's mother, Camila Corteleti, confirmed to US media that her daughter had died in the crash.Corteleti told the New York Times: "She loved the freedom. It was completely different seeing the world from the top."Filgueiras had spoken of her pride at receiving her pilot's licence while still a senior in high school in an interview with a local affiliate of CBS News in 2023."I like being different than everyone," she said. "Some people think that it's weird that I can fly planes but I can't drive a car - I mean, I can, but a lot of people think it's funny."A spokesperson for East Coast Jets, where pilot Jeff Gregory used to work, said: "We are deeply saddened to learn that Capt Jeff Gregory was among those who lost their lives in yesterday's tragic aviation accident in Palm Beach."He was married with two children, US media report.

schema.headline: Florida plane crash investigators say jet may have broken apart before impact as family named
